ethics_check.title: Ethics Approval Check
ethics_check.summary_text: All papers that appeared to involve live data collection contained an ethics approval statement.

table.text: GLMMs with random slopes only for participants were favored by AIC and BIC, but inflated Type I error rates for interactions by ignoring item-specific variability in the repetition effect.
In a second phase, previously seen statements are intermixed with novel statements, and participants are asked to judge the truthfulness of each statement.
table.header: Analyzing Binary Judgments: An Empirical and Simulation-Based Comparison of Aggregated and Trial-Level Approaches for Hypothesis Testing

table.text: Subjects were assigned correlated random intercepts and random slopes for repetition and status (u 0i, u 1i, u 2i ), and items were assigned correlated random intercepts and random slopes for repetition (v 0j, v 1j ).

Doubling the number of items had the strongest effect on the non-manipulated parameters of intercept and status estimates, whereas doubling the number of participants had a larger effect on the repetition estimates.

Regarding the random-effects structure of GLMMs, both studies showed that random slopes of repetition for subjects are essential, which provides converging evidence with previous studies showing pronounced interindividual differences in the truth effect (Schnuerch et al., 2021; Zajdler & Schnuerch, 2026).
table.formatted: Regarding the random-effects structure of GLMMs, both studies showed that random slopes of repetition for subjects are essential, which provides converging evidence with previous studies showing pronounced interindividual differences in the truth effect <ref type="bibr" target="#b85">(Schnuerch et al., 2021;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b99">Zajdler & Schnuerch, 2026)</ref>.

ethics_check.report:
Based on the following text, we would expect an ethics approval statement, and it was present:

> GLMMs with random slopes only for participants were favored by AIC and BIC, but inflated Type I error rates for interactions by ignoring item-specific variability in the repetition effect.

> In a second phase, previously seen statements are intermixed with novel statements, and participants are asked to judge the truthfulness of each statement.

> Subjects were assigned correlated random intercepts and random slopes for repetition and status (u 0i, u 1i, u 2i ), and items were assigned correlated random intercepts and random slopes for repetition (v 0j, v 1j ).

> Doubling the number of items had the strongest effect on the non-manipulated parameters of intercept and status estimates, whereas doubling the number of participants had a larger effect on the repetition estimates.

> Regarding the random-effects structure of GLMMs, both studies showed that random slopes of repetition for subjects are essential, which provides converging evidence with previous studies showing pronounced interindividual differences in the truth effect (Schnuerch et al., 2021; Zajdler & Schnuerch, 2026).

Ethics approval statement:

> Ethics approval: Not applicable.

power.title: Power Analysis Check

table.text: The two-step SDT approach also showed comparable power with the GLMMs (.634 -.986). The models with the best-calibrated Type I error (2RS, 3RS, and CRI) showed power for the interaction (.608 -.981) comparable to, though marginally lower than, RS and RSS, indicating that stricter control over Type I error did not come at a substantial cost to power once the number of subjects reached 100. Note that the higher power of RS and RSS for the interaction partly reflects their inflated Type I error rates. As for Type I error rates, power was computed across all replications, including singular fits, which occurred most often for 2RS, 3RS, and CRI. Overall, this should be considered when weighing these models' suitability to specific applications, since high singularity rate limits the practical applicability of otherwise well-calibrated models in real datasets with comparable sample sizes.

You reported a power analysis that has been classified as 'post-hoc'. Calculating observed power is [almost never useful](https://lakens.github.io/statistical_inferences/08-samplesizejustification.html#sec-posthocpower). If you actually performed a sensitivity power analysis, label it as such explicitly.

```{r} #| echo: false # table data -------------------------------------- table <- structure(list(text = "The two-step SDT approach also showed comparable power with the GLMMs (.634 -.986). The models with the best-calibrated Type I error (2RS, 3RS, and CRI) showed power for the interaction (.608 -.981) comparable to, though marginally lower than, RS and RSS, indicating that stricter control over Type I error did not come at a substantial cost to power once the number of subjects reached 100. Note that the higher power of RS and RSS for the interaction partly reflects their inflated Type I error rates. As for Type I error rates, power was computed across all replications, including singular fits, which occurred most often for 2RS, 3RS, and CRI. Overall, this should be considered when weighing these models' suitability to specific applications, since high singularity rate limits the practical applicability of otherwise well-calibrated models in real datasets with comparable sample sizes."), row.names = c(NA, -1L), class = c("tbl_df", "tbl", "data.frame")) # display table ----------------------------------- metacheck::report_table(table, "auto", 5, FALSE) ```

::: {.callout-tip title="Learn More" collapse="true"}

Power analyses need to contain the following information to be interpretable: the type of power analysis, the statistical test, the software used, sample size, critical alpha criterion, power level, effect size, and an effect size metric. In addition, it is recommended to make sure the power analysis is reproducible (by sharing the code, or a screenshot, of the power analysis), and to provide good arguments for why the study was designed to detect an effect of this size.

For an a-priori power analysis, where the sample size is determined, reporting all information would look like:

> An a priori power analysis for an independent samples t-test, conducted using the pwr.t.test function from pwr (Champely, 2020), indicated that for a Cohen's d = 0.5, an alpha level of 0.05, and a desired power level of 80% required at least 64 participants in each group.

For a sensitivity power analysis, this sentence would look like:

> A sensitivity power analysis for an independent samples t-test, conducted using the pwr.t.test function from pwr (Champely, 2020), indicated that with 64 participants in each group, and an alpha level of 0.05, a desired power level of 80% was reached for an effect size of d = 0.5.

:::

codebook_check.title: Codebook Check
codebook_check.summary_text:
-  We parsed 21 variable definitions from codebook/README files.
-  57 of 577 data columns (10%) are documented in a codebook; 520 are not.
-  A codebook was found and parsed (21 variable definitions), but its variable names do not match the data columns, so the documentation could not be linked automatically (only 10% of columns matched). For example, the codebook documents ``subject``, ``statement``, ``repetition`` while the data has `subject`, `statement`, `repetition`. This often means the data holds computed scores or subscales while the codebook lists the underlying items. To make the codebook usable automatically, document variables under the exact names used in the data file (one row per data column), with a label and, for rating items, the response scale.

report: This module checks whether each extracted data column is documented in a codebook or README, and flags documented variables that never appear in the data.
We examined 3 codebook/README/label sources and 577 data columns across 64 files.

**A codebook was found and parsed (21 variable definitions), but its variable names do not match the data columns, so the documentation could not be linked automatically (only 10% of columns matched). For example, the codebook documents ``subject``, ``statement``, ``repetition`` while the data has `subject`, `statement`, `repetition`. This often means the data holds computed scores or subscales while the codebook lists the underlying items. To make the codebook usable automatically, document variables under the exact names used in the data file (one row per data column), with a label and, for rating items, the response scale.**

-  We classified 104 files: 66 data, 12 code, 26 documentation.
-  We found 66 tabular data files and extracted 577 columns from 64 of them.

Such files need R (and the exact packages used) to open and are not machine-readable. Share the underlying data as CSV (or a documented `.sav`/`.dta`) with a codebook so it can be reused without R: full-results.Rda. We ran automated data-quality checks on 577 columns; 52 columns have at least one potential issue (38 columns with values in a legacy (non-UTF-8) encoding; 14 columns whose name contains file-illegal characters or is excessively long; 3 columns with leading/trailing whitespace).

#### Careless Responding
No file could be screened for careless responding.

**What this does not cover.** Only 0 of 64 data files could be screened: the rest had no detectable multi-item scale block, or too few respondents. Even in a screened file, these checks only look at multi-item rating scales — the only place where a repeated or flat answer pattern is interpretable. Single questions, open text, demographics and any item outside a detected scale block are never examined. A respondent can therefore answer most of a survey carelessly and still not be flagged here, and finding nothing is not evidence that a dataset is free of careless responding.

reproducibility_check.title: Reproducibility Check
reproducibility_check.summary_text:
-  We assessed AND ran 12 R code files for reproducibility (each in an isolated Docker container).
-  3 of 7 scripts ran without error when executed (5 more are run by another script with `source()`).
-  15 installable dependencies detected.
- 1225 statistics stored from the extracted output; 0 of 26 reported tests matched (0%).

live_data_statements: GLMMs with random slopes only for participants were favored by AIC and BIC, but inflated Type I error rates for interactions by ignoring item-specific variability in the repetition effect.
In a second phase, previously seen statements are intermixed with novel statements, and participants are asked to judge the truthfulness of each statement.

Subjects were assigned correlated random intercepts and random slopes for repetition and status (u 0i, u 1i, u 2i ), and items were assigned correlated random intercepts and random slopes for repetition (v 0j, v 1j ).

Doubling the number of items had the strongest effect on the non-manipulated parameters of intercept and status estimates, whereas doubling the number of participants had a larger effect on the repetition estimates.

Regarding the random-effects structure of GLMMs, both studies showed that random slopes of repetition for subjects are essential, which provides converging evidence with previous studies showing pronounced interindividual differences in the truth effect (Schnuerch et al., 2021; Zajdler & Schnuerch, 2026).

report: This module assesses whether the paper's code could be run on its data, and — because `execute = TRUE` — **actually ran it**. We examined 12 R code files.
#### Run order
The scripts were ordered by their data dependencies (a script writing a file another reads runs first), `source()` calls, and numeric filename prefixes.

```{r}
#| echo: false


# table data --------------------------------------
table <- structure(list(Order = 1:12, File = c("analysis_functions.R", 
"data_generation.R", "database.R", "datasets.R", "parallelization.R", 
"analyses.Rmd", "interpretation.Rmd", "run_simulation.R", "extract_results.Rmd", 
"sdt-plot.Rmd", "simulation_parameters.R", "working-example.R"
), "Runs after" = c("—", "—", "—", "—", "—", "database.R, datasets.R, parallelization.R", 
"analyses.Rmd", "data_generation.R, analysis_functions.R", "run_simulation.R", 
"—", "analyses.Rmd", "—"), Basis = c("none", "none", "none", 
"none", "none", "dependency", "dependency", "dependency", "dependency", 
"none", "dependency", "none")), row.names = c(NA, -12L), class = "data.frame")

# display table -----------------------------------
metacheck::report_table(table, "auto", 10, FALSE)
```
#### File paths

**1 data path in the code does not work in the repository as deposited.** We pointed it to where the file is, so the code could run: `/Users/semih/Downloads/results.Rda` to `../results.Rda` (in simulation_parameters.R). The code should be changed, because as written it does not find the file.
#### Files not run on their own
3 files only define functions, so running them on their own says nothing: a function counts when a script uses it. These files are not counted as scripts. 0 are used by no script in the deposit.

```{r}
#| echo: false


# table data --------------------------------------
table <- structure(list(File = c("parallelization.R", "analysis_functions.R", 
"data_generation.R"), "Used by" = c("analyses.Rmd", "run_simulation.R", 
"run_simulation.R")), row.names = c(NA, -3L), class = "data.frame")

# display table -----------------------------------
metacheck::report_table(table, "auto", 10, FALSE)
```
#### Execution

**The code was run.** Each script ran in an isolated Docker container against a throwaway copy of the repository, in the run order above, with a 300-second per-script timeout. Of 10 scripts: 3 ran without error, 0 errored, 2 timed out, 0 could not run because one of its own dependencies is unavailable, 0 did not parse, and 5 were run by another script with `source()`. Running against current package versions: a break can reflect version drift, which argues for pinning versions. **2 scripts could not be tried, because a file they need was not downloaded**: interpretation.Rmd, simulation_parameters.R. They are not counted as scripts that did not reproduce. The file: results.Rda (725.3 MB); files over 100 MB are not downloaded.

```{r}
#| echo: false


# table data --------------------------------------
table <- structure(list(File = c("analysis_functions.R", "data_generation.R", 
"database.R", "datasets.R", "parallelization.R", "analyses.Rmd", 
"interpretation.Rmd", "run_simulation.R", "extract_results.Rmd", 
"sdt-plot.Rmd", "simulation_parameters.R", "working-example.R"
), Outcome = c("run_by_source", "run_by_source", "run_by_source", 
"run_by_source", "run_by_source", "timed_out", "not_downloaded", 
"timed_out", "ran_ok", "ran_ok", "not_downloaded", "ran_ok"), 
    Detail = c("", "", "", "", "", "timeout", "", "timeout", 
    "", "", "", ""), "Time (s)" = c(0, 0, 0, 0, 0, 300.3, 1.9, 
    300.3, 22.2, 1.3, 2.5, 9)), row.names = c(NA, -12L), class = "data.frame")

# display table -----------------------------------
metacheck::report_table(table, "auto", 15, FALSE)
```
**`setwd()` in the code**

**1 script calls `setwd()`.** This is bad practice: it hardcodes where the code must run (often an absolute path on the author's own machine) and breaks the moment the code is run anywhere else. To run the code we replaced these calls with a statement that does nothing. Any such script that then ran is **reproducible only after ignoring a `setwd()` that should not have been in the code and needs to be fixed**.

```{r}
#| echo: false


# table data --------------------------------------
table <- structure(list(File = "run_simulation.R", "setwd() removed" = 1L, 
    "Path(s) it set" = "~/GLMM/simulation"), row.names = c(NA, 
-1L), class = "data.frame")

# display table -----------------------------------
metacheck::report_table(table, "auto", 10, FALSE)
```
**Run by another script**

5 scripts are run by another script with `source()`, so they were not run on their own: each script runs in a fresh R process, and on their own a sourced script lacks the packages and objects the sourcing script sets up first. Their outcome is part of the sourcing script's outcome.

```{r}
#| echo: false


# table data --------------------------------------
table <- structure(list(File = c("database.R", "datasets.R", "parallelization.R", 
"data_generation.R", "analysis_functions.R"), "Run by" = c("analyses.Rmd", 
"analyses.Rmd", "analyses.Rmd", "run_simulation.R", "run_simulation.R"
)), row.names = c("database.R", "datasets.R", "parallelization.R", 
"data_generation.R", "analysis_functions.R"), class = "data.frame")

# display table -----------------------------------
metacheck::report_table(table, "auto", 10, FALSE)
```

info.title: Analyzing Binary Judgments: An Empirical and Simulation-Based Comparison of Aggregated and Trial-Level Approaches for Hypothesis Testing

text.text: Binary judgments are widely used in psychological research to investigate cognitive processes and decision making.

Statistical approaches for analyzing such data differ in whether responses are aggregated (e.g., analysis of variance, ANOVA) or modeled at the trial level (e.g., generalized linear mixed models, GLMMs), and in whether results are interpreted as choice proportions or in terms of signal detection theory (SDT) parameters for response bias and discrimination ability.
We examined how these approaches differ in specification, interpretation, and results.

First, we reanalyzed 20 openly available datasets on the illusory truth effect (212,555 observations), comparing by-subjects (F1) and by-items (F2) ANOVAs of choice proportions, their combination via min-F ′ , a two-step SDT approach (ANOVA of individual SDT estimates), and seven GLMMs with random-effects structures of varying complexity.
Second, a Monte Carlo simulation assessed Type I error rates, power, and parameter recovery.
GLMMs with random slopes for both participants and items controlled Type I error rates best but often resulted in singular fits.
GLMMs with random slopes only for participants were favored by AIC and BIC, but inflated Type I error rates for interactions by ignoring item-specific variability in the repetition effect.
Random-intercept-only GLMMs, F1 and F2 ANOVA, and two-step SDT were too liberal for some effects, whereas min-F ′ was overly conservative.
Unlike aggregated analyses, GLMMs account for both participant and item variability and estimate SDT parameters with less bias.
We therefore recommend GLMMs with theoretically justified random-effects structure, simplified only if necessary and with the resulting risk of Type I errors for confirmatory hypothesis testing.

Binary judgment tasks, where individuals select between two response options, such as true and false, yes and no, like and dislike, or ethical and unethical, are central for studying decision-making processes across psychological domains.
These tasks serve as controlled paradigms to investigate how individuals assess the veracity, acceptability, or ethicality of information.
However, researchers face many degrees of freedom when analyzing binary data.

The available approaches differ (1) in the level of analysis-whether they model aggregated choice proportions or responses at the trial-level-and (2) in their analytic focus-whether they focus on response probabilities or on response bias and discrimination ability.

As a case study, we focus on the illusory truth effect, a robust phenomenon in cognitive psychology often studied using binary judgments: repeated exposure to a statement increases its perceived truthfulness, regardless of its truth status (Hasher et al., 1977).
text.formatted: As a case study, we focus on the illusory truth effect, a robust phenomenon in cognitive psychology often studied using binary judgments: repeated exposure to a statement increases its perceived truthfulness, regardless of its truth status <ref type="bibr" target="#b38">(Hasher et al., 1977)</ref>.

text.text: This cognitive bias has often been replicated (Dechêne et al., 2010; Henderson et al., 2022) and holds significant implications for belief formation and misinformation research (Pennycook et al., 2018).
text.formatted: This cognitive bias has often been replicated <ref type="bibr" target="#b25">(Dechêne et al., 2010;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b42">Henderson et al., 2022)</ref> and holds significant implications for belief formation and misinformation research <ref type="bibr" target="#b75">(Pennycook et al., 2018)</ref>.

text.text: Typical experimental paradigms investigating the truth effect present participants with a set of statements in the first phase.
In a second phase, previously seen statements are intermixed with novel statements, and participants are asked to judge the truthfulness of each statement.

Experimental designs often include additional manipulations, such as variations in repetition frequency, alterations in source credibility, modifications in contextual framing, or manipulations of statement properties (e.g., Alter & Oppenheimer, 2009; Schmidt & Heck, 2024).
text.formatted: Experimental designs often include additional manipulations, such as variations in repetition frequency, alterations in source credibility, modifications in contextual framing, or manipulations of statement properties (e.g., <ref type="bibr" target="#b2">Alter & Oppenheimer, 2009;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b83">Schmidt & Heck, 2024)</ref>.

text.text: We are interested in data structures where the dependent variable are binary responses (e.g., true/false judgments) gathered across multiple statements and participants under various factor levels.

Each participant evaluates multiple statements while each statement is assessed by multiple individuals, resulting in a crossed, repeated-measures design: participants and statements are fully crossed (every participant responds to each statement), and each statement is judged multiple times for each level of the repetition factor (new vs. repeated), as illustrated in Table 1.
text.formatted: Each participant evaluates multiple statements while each statement is assessed by multiple individuals, resulting in a crossed, repeated-measures design: participants and statements are fully crossed (every participant responds to each statement), and each statement is judged multiple times for each level of the repetition factor (new vs. repeated), as illustrated in Table <ref type="table" target="#tab_0">1</ref>.

text.text: This design gives rise to a crossed hierarchical structure, with observations simultaneously nested within participants and within statements.

Each subject responds to each item, and each item is presented in both the new and repeated conditions, yielding two crossed grouping factors (Subject, Item) rather than one factor being nested within the other.

Traditionally, many studies have applied repeated-measures analysis of variance (RM-ANOVA) focusing on choice proportions, which are obtained by aggregating judgments either across subjects (referred to as "F1 analysis") or across items ("F2 analysis;" Hertzog and Rovine, 1985).
text.formatted: Traditionally, many studies have applied repeated-measures analysis of variance (RM-ANOVA) focusing on choice proportions, which are obtained by aggregating judgments either across subjects (referred to as "F1 analysis") or across items ("F2 analysis;" <ref type="bibr" target="#b43">Hertzog and Rovine, 1985)</ref>.

text.text: The proportions are separately calculated for all combinations of factor levels and are used as dependent variable in two different ANOVAs.

While RM-ANOVA is a general-purpose statistical method, signal detection theory (SDT) makes assumptions about latent psychological processes, specifying how observed binary judgments are determined by individuals' discrimination ability and response bias (Green & Swets, 1966).
text.formatted: While RM-ANOVA is a general-purpose statistical method, signal detection theory (SDT) makes assumptions about latent psychological processes, specifying how observed binary judgments are determined by individuals' discrimination ability and response bias <ref type="bibr" target="#b34">(Green & Swets, 1966)</ref>.

text.text: These individual-level indexes are analyzed separately with two RM-ANOVAs, which is called the two-step SDT approach (Batailler et al., 2022).
text.formatted: These individual-level indexes are analyzed separately with two RM-ANOVAs, which is called the two-step SDT approach <ref type="bibr" target="#b8">(Batailler et al., 2022)</ref>.

text.text: More recently, generalized linear mixed models (Pinheiro & Bates, 2000) have emerged as another alternative, offering a flexible framework for modeling binary judgments at the trial-level.
text.formatted: More recently, generalized linear mixed models <ref type="bibr" target="#b76">(Pinheiro & Bates, 2000)</ref> have emerged as another alternative, offering a flexible framework for modeling binary judgments at the trial-level.

text.text: GLMMs accommodate random effects for subjects and items simultaneously, allowing researchers to model crossed hierarchical data.
The different analysis approaches for binary judgments share common underlying principles, while offering distinct benefits and drawbacks.

However, for substantive researchers, differences and similarities in the specification, application, and interpretation of methods with different aggregation levels (aggregation vs. trial-level) and analytic focus (choice proportions vs.
SDT) may not be clear.
Introductory and conceptual papers have mainly focused on linear mixed models (DeBruine & Barr, 2021; Judd et al., 2012).
text.formatted: Introductory and conceptual papers have mainly focused on linear mixed models <ref type="bibr" target="#b23">(DeBruine & Barr, 2021;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b49">Judd et al., 2012)</ref>.

text.text: Similarly, studies comparing the performance of ANOVA and GLMMs have typically used simulations with linear models (e.g., Baayen et al., 2008; Barr, 2008; Scandola & Tidoni, 2024).
text.formatted: Similarly, studies comparing the performance of ANOVA and GLMMs have typically used simulations with linear models (e.g., <ref type="bibr" target="#b4">Baayen et al., 2008;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b6">Barr, 2008;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b82">Scandola & Tidoni, 2024)</ref>.

text.text: Mixed models for binary data such as logistic models have been assessed using exemplary datasets (Jaeger, 2008; Quené & van den Bergh, 2008).
text.formatted: Mixed models for binary data such as logistic models have been assessed using exemplary datasets <ref type="bibr" target="#b46">(Jaeger, 2008;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b77">Quené & van den Bergh, 2008)</ref>.

text.text: We are not aware of systematic comparisons of analysis methods for binary judgments across a larger set of real datasets.
Hence, it is unclear whether inferences from one method are robust when using alternative methods and how such differences affect the interpretation of results (Steegen et al., 2016).

text.text: This gap leads to our central research question: How exactly and to what extent does the choice of analysis method impact the conclusions derived from binary judgment data?
To address this question, we first compare the assumptions and practical implementation of different methods for binary data.

We assume that certain fixed effects (e.g., repetition and truth status of the presented statements) are of substantive interest due to theoretical and design reasons, and are thus included in all models.
Here, we investigate confirmatory hypothesis testing of these fixed effects.
By comparing the methods both in a large-scale, empirical reanalysis and a simulation study, we seek to provide practical guidance for their application in psychological research.
We focus on the truth effect as a case study because it is a robust effect (Dechêne et al., 2010) for which many datasets are openly available.
text.formatted: We focus on the truth effect as a case study because it is a robust effect <ref type="bibr" target="#b25">(Dechêne et al., 2010)</ref> for which many datasets are openly available.

text.text: The robustness of the effect ensures that instabilities or anomalies in the analyses are less likely to be artifacts of noisy data or unreliable study designs, but more likely reflect relevant differences between the different analysis approaches.

Methods for binary judgments can be broadly framed along two dimensions: (1) the aggregation level at which data are analyzed (i.e., aggregated proportions or trial-wise responses), and (2) the analytic focus (i.e., effects on choice probabilities or SDT parameters).
We illustrate all methods using a typical dataset investigating the truth effect by Nadarevic and Erdfelder (2025), which includes the factors repetition and truth status.

text.text: With respect to the first dimension, RM-ANOVA and two-step SDT operate on data aggregated across trials, typically in the form of response proportions or SDT parameters estimated separately for each participant and condition.
In contrast, GLMMs model each response per trial as a function of the experimental design and can account for variability in participants and items simultaneously.
With respect to the second dimension, the methods differ in whether they focus on raw choice proportions or on SDT constructs.
In truth-effect studies, RM-ANOVA typically focuses on the effect of experimental factors on the probability of responding "true."

In contrast, the two-step SDT approach and GLMMs focus on the effect of factors on response bias (the general tendency to favor one response over another) and discrimination ability (how well the stimulus categories can be distinguished).
Analysis of variance (ANOVA) is the standard approach for testing differences in means across two or more groups or conditions (Fisher, 1970).
text.formatted: Analysis of variance (ANOVA) is the standard approach for testing differences in means across two or more groups or conditions <ref type="bibr" target="#b30">(Fisher, 1970)</ref>.

text.text: Repeated-measures ANOVA is a widely used general-purpose technique that is also commonly applied to aggregated binary judgments in designs with within-subject factors or multiple time points.
In typical truth effect experiments, each participant judges the truth of multiple new and repeated statements.
Responses are first aggregated within each person for each condition to determine the proportion of new and repeated statements judged as true.
The proportions Y i1 and Y i2 for each person i are then treated as repeated measures data (Cochran, 1940; Jaeger, 2008).
text.formatted: The proportions Y i1 and Y i2 for each person i are then treated as repeated measures data <ref type="bibr" target="#b19">(Cochran, 1940;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b46">Jaeger, 2008)</ref>.

text.text: ANOVA can be conceptualized as a general linear model with groups, conditions, and subjects (or items) serving as categorical predictors.
In repeated-measures designs, the observed proportion of "true" judgments for subject i in condition j (new vs. repeated) is modeled as where µ is the overall grand mean across all proportions.
The term β j represents the effect of repetition, while u i accounts for subject-specific deviations from the grand mean.
The residual error, ϵ ij , captures the variability neither explained by subject nor condition (Ståhle & Wold, 1989).

text.text: ANOVA is widely used for binary judgments, yet its application to choice proportions has several limitations.
First, the normality assumption is violated, as the dependent variable does not have continuous, unbounded values that are normally distributed within each level of the within-subjects factor.

Instead, choice proportions are bounded between 0 and 1, and fitting standard linear regression models (including ANOVA as a special case) can lead to impossible predictions and confidence intervals beyond these bounds (Blanton & Jaccard, 2006; Jaeger, 2008).
text.formatted: Instead, choice proportions are bounded between 0 and 1, and fitting standard linear regression models (including ANOVA as a special case) can lead to impossible predictions and confidence intervals beyond these bounds <ref type="bibr" target="#b13">(Blanton & Jaccard, 2006;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b46">Jaeger, 2008)</ref>.

text.text: Moreover, residuals do not satisfy the assumption of variance homogeneity.

While between-subjects ANOVA for dichotomous responses is robust under certain conditions (e.g., equal cell frequencies; Lunney, 1970), it is not clear whether this also holds in the case of crossed random effects.

text.text: However, the transformation does not fully resolve the issue of boundedness, often resulting in confidence intervals exceeding the theoretical limits (Jaeger, 2008).

text.text: Repeated-measures ANOVA should also meet the sphericity assumption of equal variances of the differences between all pairs of conditions.

When this assumption is violated, which is more likely the case for choice proportions, the F -statistics can become too liberal, increasing the likelihood of Type I errors (McCall & Appelbaum, 1973).

text.text: Sphericity is typically tested using Mauchly's test (Mauchly, 1940), and if violated, corrections such as the Greenhouse-Geisser (Greenhouse & Geisser, 1959) or Huynh-Feldt adjustments (Huynh & Feldt, 1976) are applied to the degrees of freedom to improve accuracy (Tabachnick & Fidell, 2007).

text.text: The aggregation of binary judgments into choice proportions introduces additional biases and fallacies.
Idiosyncrasies of the item content can result in a violation of the ANOVA assumption that choice proportions are conditionally independent within each person.
The language-as-fixed-effect fallacy arises when pooling data masks critical item-level variability which can lead to biased estimates (Baayen et al., 2002; Clark, 1973).
text.formatted: The language-as-fixed-effect fallacy arises when pooling data masks critical item-level variability which can lead to biased estimates <ref type="bibr" target="#b5">(Baayen et al., 2002;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b18">Clark, 1973)</ref>.

text.text: Aggregation often distorts estimates by ignoring unmodeled variability, which results in asymptotic bias (Ashby et al., 1994; Estes, 1956; Richter, 2006) and exacerbates violations of the independence assumption (Curran & Hintzman, 1995).
text.formatted: Aggregation often distorts estimates by ignoring unmodeled variability, which results in asymptotic bias <ref type="bibr" target="#b3">(Ashby et al., 1994;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b27">Estes, 1956;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b78">Richter, 2006)</ref> and exacerbates violations of the independence assumption <ref type="bibr" target="#b21">(Curran & Hintzman, 1995)</ref>.

text.text: For instance, ANOVA neglects variability of the truth effect across items due to differences in the plausibility or complexity of the presented statements.
Moreover, if binary judgments are missing in some conditions, the corresponding choice proportions will have larger error variances, resulting in variance heterogeneity.
Even more, subjects have to be excluded from the dataset if they do not have observations in one of the conditions.
However, such exclusions reduce statistical power and may introduce systematic biases.
As a result, small numbers of trials per condition can increase the risk of artifact-driven results (Levine et al., 2022).
text.formatted: As a result, small numbers of trials per condition can increase the risk of artifact-driven results <ref type="bibr" target="#b53">(Levine et al., 2022)</ref>.

text.text: Repeated-measures ANOVA does not allow for the simultaneous modeling of subject-and item-level variability.

As a remedy, to account for systematic differences between items, data can be aggregated across persons within each item using a so-called "F2 ANOVA" (whereas the aggregation across items within persons has been termed "F1 ANOVA; " Clark, 1973).

Signal detection theory (SDT) is a framework for measuring individuals' ability to discern signal and noise under uncertainty (Green & Swets, 1966; Wixted, 2020).
text.formatted: Signal detection theory (SDT) is a framework for measuring individuals' ability to discern signal and noise under uncertainty <ref type="bibr" target="#b34">(Green & Swets, 1966;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b97">Wixted, 2020)</ref>.

text.text: According to SDT, an individual's performance to detect a signal depends on their discrimination ability and on the adopted decision criterion, which may be influenced by factors such as expectations and the potential consequences of their choices (Green & Swets, 1966).

text.text: SDT provides a method for separating a person's sensitivity to discriminate signals from noise while accounting for response biases in favor of one response option (N. Macmillan & Creelman, 2004).

text.text: On each trial, a signal is sampled at random either from the noise or the signal distribution for false and true statements, respectively.

The discrimination ability d ′ (also called sensitivity) quantifies the separation between these two distributions in standard deviation units, with higher values indicating better discrimination ability.
If the signal exceeds a certain decision threshold, the statement is judged as true; otherwise, it is judged as false.
The response bias c (also called criterion) is defined as the distance from the midpoints of the noise and signal distributions to the threshold.
A neutral response bias (c = 0) correspond to equal miss and false alarm rates, implying no predisposition toward either response option.
In contrast, positive values of c suggest a conservative bias, whereby more evidence is required to judge a statement as true, resulting in fewer false alarms but more misses.

Conversely, negative c values reflect a liberal bias, with a greater tendency to judge statements as true, thereby increasing both hits and false alarms (N. Macmillan & Creelman, 2004; Stanislaw & Todorov, 1999).

Next, these categories are aggregated separately per person and condition to obtain hit and false alarm rates.
Note that the miss and correct-rejection rates are not required as the two proportions for true statements and the two proportions for false statements each have to sum to one.

Generalized linear mixed models (GLMMs) extend traditional regression models for non-normally distributed dependent variables (Bates et al., 2015; Pinheiro & Bates, 2000).

text.text: GLMMs model binary judgments at the trial-level and assume that each response follows a
Bernoulli distribution (or equivalently, a binomial distribution with only one observation).

While fixed effects account for the effects of experimental factors or covariates, the inclusion of random effects enables modeling dependencies stemming from different sources (e.g., from persons and items).

The mixed-effects framework is particularly valuable for fully crossed experimental designs, where variation exists across subjects and items (Epifania et al., 2024; Singmann & Kellen, 2019).

text.text: Accounting for both sources of variance is especially relevant in areas with qualitative differences between stimuli such as the truth effect, where statements differ in plausibility, syntactic complexity, and difficulty (Aktepe & Heck, 2025).
text.formatted: Accounting for both sources of variance is especially relevant in areas with qualitative differences between stimuli such as the truth effect, where statements differ in plausibility, syntactic complexity, and difficulty <ref type="bibr" target="#b1">(Aktepe & Heck, 2025)</ref>.

text.text: Thereby, GLMMs address a critical limitation of methods requiring an aggregation of binary judgments either across items within person (as in F1 ANOVA and two-step SDT) or across persons within item (as in F2 ANOVA; Baayen et al., 2008; Bates et al., 2015).
text.formatted: Thereby, GLMMs address a critical limitation of methods requiring an aggregation of binary judgments either across items within person (as in F1 ANOVA and two-step SDT) or across persons within item (as in F2 ANOVA; <ref type="bibr" target="#b4">Baayen et al., 2008;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b10">Bates et al., 2015)</ref>.

text.text: The GLMM approach also circumvents scale distortions introduced when fitting nonlinear models to aggregated data (Estes, 1956).
text.formatted: The GLMM approach also circumvents scale distortions introduced when fitting nonlinear models to aggregated data <ref type="bibr" target="#b27">(Estes, 1956)</ref>.

text.text: GLMMs naturally accommodate unbalanced designs and missing responses without requiring data imputation (Baayen et al., 2008; Pinheiro & Bates, 2000).
text.formatted: GLMMs naturally accommodate unbalanced designs and missing responses without requiring data imputation <ref type="bibr" target="#b4">(Baayen et al., 2008;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b76">Pinheiro & Bates, 2000)</ref>.

text.text: Moreover, GLMMs automatically implement partial pooling and shrinkage.
Partial pooling refers to using information from the group to inform parameter estimates at the individual level, which reduces the variance in parameter estimates (Quené & van den Bergh, 2008).
text.formatted: Partial pooling refers to using information from the group to inform parameter estimates at the individual level, which reduces the variance in parameter estimates <ref type="bibr" target="#b77">(Quené & van den Bergh, 2008)</ref>.

text.text: This results in shrinkage, meaning that extreme estimates are systematically pulled towards the overall mean, preventing overfitting and yielding more reliable estimates (McElreath, 2018).
text.formatted: This results in shrinkage, meaning that extreme estimates are systematically pulled towards the overall mean, preventing overfitting and yielding more reliable estimates <ref type="bibr" target="#b63">(McElreath, 2018)</ref>.

text.text: GLMMs can be specified in a manner to implement SDT within a mixed-effects framework, allowing researchers to focus on discrimination ability and response bias while accounting for complex dependencies.

For this purpose, it is necessary to model binary judgments by a GLMM with a probit link function, g(p) = Φ -1 (p), while including the actual status of the items as a contrast-coded predictor (+0.5 = "true," -0.5 = "false;" for tutorials, see Samara, 2026; Zloteanu & Vuorre, 2024).
text.formatted: For this purpose, it is necessary to model binary judgments by a GLMM with a probit link function, g(p) = Φ -1 (p), while including the actual status of the items as a contrast-coded predictor (+0.5 = "true," -0.5 = "false;" for tutorials, see <ref type="bibr" target="#b81">Samara, 2026;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b100">Zloteanu & Vuorre, 2024)</ref>.

text.text: As a result, the estimated intercept corresponds to the negative response bias (-c) in SDT, while the estimated coefficient for the actual item status corresponds to the discrimination ability parameter d ′ (DeCarlo, 1998; Rouder & Lu, 2005).
text.formatted: As a result, the estimated intercept corresponds to the negative response bias (-c) in SDT, while the estimated coefficient for the actual item status corresponds to the discrimination ability parameter d ′ <ref type="bibr" target="#b24">(DeCarlo, 1998;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b79">Rouder & Lu, 2005)</ref>.

text.text: Intuitively, this is due to the fact that a larger intercept generally results in a higher predicted probability of responding "true," whereas a larger slope for truth status results in a larger difference in the response probabilities for true and false statements.
The effect of other factors (e.g., repetition) on the response bias c can be modeled by including main effects in the matrix X (e.g., a column with +0.5 = repeated, -0.5 = new).

A positive main effect of repetition means that repeated statements are more likely to receive "true" responses overall, corresponding to a lower c (i.e., a more liberal criterion) for repeated than for new statements.
This is exactly the result in our empirical example in Table 2, where the estimate for the repetition effect is already multiplied by -1 to facilitate interpretation in terms of c.
text.formatted: This is exactly the result in our empirical example in Table <ref type="table" target="#tab_1">2</ref>, where the estimate for the repetition effect is already multiplied by -1 to facilitate interpretation in terms of c.

text.text: The estimate -0.40 (SE = 0.05) is very similar to the one from the two-step SDT approach.
While additive effects correspond to effects on c, multiplicative interaction terms with item status can be included to test whether factors moderate the discrimination ability d ′ .
For instance, a positive repetition-status interaction term would indicate that repetition improves discrimination between true and false statements.
In our empirical example in Table 2, this interaction was not significant.
text.formatted: In our empirical example in Table <ref type="table" target="#tab_1">2</ref>, this interaction was not significant.

text.text: Random effects in GLMMs also carry substantive interpretation within the SDT framework.
Random intercepts for subjects and items reflect subject-and item-specific differences in the response criterion (c).
Random slopes for repetition by subject capture person-specific differences in the strength of the repetition effect on the response bias c.
Similarly, random slopes for truth status reflect subject variability in sensitivity (d ′ ), indicating that discrimination ability differs rather than being fixed at the population level.
By adding random slopes of the repetition-status interaction for subjects, one can account for subject-specific variation in the effect of repetition on d ′.
Despite offering many advantages, GLMMs also come with practical challenges.
Their estimation can be computationally costly and prone to singular fits, especially when assuming complex random effects structures (Barr et al., 2013; Jaeger et al., 2011).
text.formatted: Their estimation can be computationally costly and prone to singular fits, especially when assuming complex random effects structures <ref type="bibr" target="#b7">(Barr et al., 2013;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b47">Jaeger et al., 2011)</ref>.

text.text: Bayesian mixed models are less prone to convergence and singularity issues and may allow stable estimation of more complex hierarchical structures (Bürkner, 2017; Gelman et al., 2020).
text.formatted: Bayesian mixed models are less prone to convergence and singularity issues and may allow stable estimation of more complex hierarchical structures <ref type="bibr" target="#b15">(Bürkner, 2017;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b33">Gelman et al., 2020)</ref>.

text.text: Irrespective of whether mixed models are fitted in a frequentist or Bayesian way (for a comparison, see Dalla Bona et al., 2026), specifying the optimal random effects structure remains contentious, with ongoing debates over whether "maximal" models (Barr et al., 2013) or parsimonious models (Bates et al., 2018; Matuschek et al., 2017) are better at balancing Type I error and statistical power.
text.formatted: Irrespective of whether mixed models are fitted in a frequentist or Bayesian way (for a comparison, see Dalla Bona et al., 2026), specifying the optimal random effects structure remains contentious, with ongoing debates over whether "maximal" models <ref type="bibr" target="#b7">(Barr et al., 2013)</ref> or parsimonious models <ref type="bibr" target="#b9">(Bates et al., 2018;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b60">Matuschek et al., 2017)</ref> are better at balancing Type I error and statistical power.

text.text: Maximal GLMMs account for all possible sources of variance in a study (e.g., persons and items) by including corresponding random intercepts and random slopes for all predictor variables.

Such models can be empirically unidentifiable when there is insufficient data to estimate their parameters, in turn requiring a very large number of observations for convergence and non-singular fits (Jaeger et al., 2011).
text.formatted: Such models can be empirically unidentifiable when there is insufficient data to estimate their parameters, in turn requiring a very large number of observations for convergence and non-singular fits <ref type="bibr" target="#b47">(Jaeger et al., 2011)</ref>.

text.text: In contrast, parsimonious models include random slopes only for some predictors and some sources of variance based on prior knowledge and theoretical considerations, which facilitates model fitting.
We explain the specification and interpretation of different random-effects structures for factorial designs in the next section.

Note that the selection of which fixed effects to include in a GLMM is beyond the scope of this paper, as we assume that all experimental factors and their interactions are of interest, and thus included in all model versions (for guidance, see Bates et al., 2015; Kuznetsova et al., 2017).
text.formatted: Note that the selection of which fixed effects to include in a GLMM is beyond the scope of this paper, as we assume that all experimental factors and their interactions are of interest, and thus included in all model versions (for guidance, see <ref type="bibr" target="#b10">Bates et al., 2015;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b50">Kuznetsova et al., 2017)</ref>.

text.text: Since GLMMs for binary data lack a residual variance, their coefficients cannot easily be converted into standardized effect sizes such as Cohen's d.
As a remedy, interpretation can be facilitated by computing marginal means, which are predicted means for certain conditions averaged over all other factors in the model (Lenth, 2023).
text.formatted: As a remedy, interpretation can be facilitated by computing marginal means, which are predicted means for certain conditions averaged over all other factors in the model <ref type="bibr" target="#b52">(Lenth, 2023)</ref>.

text.text: The computation of the coefficient of determination (R² ) in GLMMs is also more intricate than in ANOVA due to the inclusion of random-effect variances, the lack of an explicit residual variance of the binomial distribution, and the non-linear link function. Nakagawa and Schielzeth (2013) proposed two types of R² for mixed models: marginal R² m , which quantifies the proportion of variance explained by the fixed effects only, and conditional R² c , which represents the proportion of variance explained by both the fixed and random effects (see also Johnson, 2014).
text.formatted: The computation of the coefficient of determination (R² ) in GLMMs is also more intricate than in ANOVA due to the inclusion of random-effect variances, the lack of an explicit residual variance of the binomial distribution, and the non-linear link function. <ref type="bibr" target="#b70">Nakagawa and Schielzeth (2013)</ref> proposed two types of R² for mixed models: marginal R² m , which quantifies the proportion of variance explained by the fixed effects only, and conditional R² c , which represents the proportion of variance explained by both the fixed and random effects (see also <ref type="bibr" target="#b48">Johnson, 2014)</ref>.

text.text: However, for singular models (i.e., if one or more random-effect variance components are estimated to be zero or are not identifiable), conditional R² c cannot be computed, as the random-effect structure does not contribute meaningfully to the model variance (Bates et al., 2015; Nakagawa et al., 2017).
text.formatted: However, for singular models (i.e., if one or more random-effect variance components are estimated to be zero or are not identifiable), conditional R² c cannot be computed, as the random-effect structure does not contribute meaningfully to the model variance <ref type="bibr" target="#b10">(Bates et al., 2015;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b69">Nakagawa et al., 2017)</ref>.

text.text: Our comparison resembles recent multiverse analyses which have been proposed for studying the robustness of results against using different methods (Harder, 2020; Steegen et al., 2016).
text.formatted: Our comparison resembles recent multiverse analyses which have been proposed for studying the robustness of results against using different methods <ref type="bibr" target="#b37">(Harder, 2020;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b92">Steegen et al., 2016)</ref>.

text.text: Specifically, we study whether and how results differ in terms of p-values and parameter estimates, as well as regarding tests of assumptions, singular fits, and model selection indices.

Standard effect sizes are not directly comparable between ANOVA and GLMMs, which estimate marginal effects on observed proportions and conditional effects on a latent probit scale without a residual variance, respectively.
We therefore compare ANOVA and GLMMs via hypothesis tests, and compare parameter estimates only between two-step SDT and GLMMs, which share the same latent scale.

Repetition was specified as a repeated-measures effect in both ANOVAs (i.e., within subjects or within items), while truth status was a within-subject effect in F1 but a between-item effect in F2 ANOVA.
The other variables were adjusted based on the specific experimental design of the studies.

text.text: In the GLMM workflow, binary truth judgments were modeled using repetition, truth status, other study-specific factors, and all interactions as independent variables.
All factors were dichotomous and coded with sum-to-zero contrasts, with one level assigned a value of -0.5 and the other 0.5.
Thereby, the corresponding coefficients can directly be interpreted as the effect of the manipulation.
Models were fitted using the glmer function from the lme4 package (Bates et al., 2015) using a probit link function.

text.text: Estimating GLMMs can be difficult because they often suffer from issues such as singular fits or converge issues.
To address these problems, we explored alternative optimization algorithms for maximum-likelihood estimation.

The default optimizer was nloptwrap in lme4's glmer function, but we additionally experimented with bobyqa, Nelder-Mead and nlminb algorithms from the optimx package (v2023-10.21) to make sure that all models were estimated properly and converged (Nash & Varadhan, 2011).

text.text: As the final numerical optimization method, we used the nlminb optimizer as it showed the fewest singularity issues across all datasets and model versions.
Note, however, that the optimizer may need to be adjusted for other datasets, as no single optimizer is universally optimal.

A singular fit means that the estimated covariance matrix of the random effects is not of full rank, for instance, because a variance is estimated to be zero or a correlation to be ±1 (Bates et al., 2015 (Bates et al., , 2018)).

text.text: Because the ground truth is unknown for empirical data, the reanalyses focus on the agreement between methods rather than on their performance, which we evaluate in the simulation study below.

To assess whether the effect of repetition generalizes not only across persons but also across statements, we compared the number of significant test results when evaluating the main effects and interactions of all factors in a study using either F1 ANOVA (aggregation across items) or F2 ANOVA (aggregation across subjects), or the min-F ′ statistic.
Figure 4 illustrates the extent to which p-values differed between these analyses.

Out of 192 tested effects, 10 were significant only in the F1 but not in the F2 ANOVA, while three were significant only in the F2 but not in the F1 ANOVA.

Aside from these minor discrepancies in statistical significance, the overall pattern remained largely consistent across F1 and F2 ANOVA, regarding both raw p-values (r = .89, 95% CI: [.85, .91] p < .001) and log p-values (r = .71, 95% CI: [.64, .78] p < .001), which shows that the results did not substantially differ between the two types of analysis.

text.text: Overall, 48 effects remained significant across all three analyses, although min-F ′ produced noticeably larger p-values.

Additionally, 10 effects that were significant in both the F1 and the F2 ANOVA were no longer significant with the min-F ′ statistic (seven of these non-significant effects involved the factor repetition and its interaction with other factors).
These findings indicate that the min-F ′ test statistic is more conservative, which results in reduced statistical power for detecting significant effects.
To evaluate the degree to which effects explain a similar amount of variance across items and across persons, we compared the coefficient of determination (R² ) obtained from the F1 and F2 ANOVA.
We observed that in 6 datasets, R² values were larger for the F1 analysis, whereas in 14 datasets, R² values were larger for the F2 analysis.
The average amount of explained variance was similar for F1 ANOVA (R² = .25, SD = .20) and F2 ANOVA (R² = .29, SD = .31).
These results indicate that the explained variance attributable to item-level differences cannot be neglected.
Moreover, Pearson's correlation analysis indicated a significant positive correlation between R² values of the F1 and F2 analyses (r = .58, 95% CI = [.19, .82], p < .001).
text.formatted: Moreover, Pearson's correlation analysis indicated a significant positive correlation between R² values of the F1 and F2 analyses (r = .58, 95% CI = [.19, .82], p < .001).

text.text: Because F1 and F2 analyses aggregate judgments either by subject or by item, respectively, the results should be interpreted with caution.

The results do not imply the superiority of one analysis over the other, but rather highlight the relevance of differences between statements while providing evidence for the robustness of conclusions.

Finally, ANOVA relies on several statistical assumptions, including homogeneous error variances, which is typically assessed using Levene's test, and normally distributed residuals, evaluated using the Shapiro-Wilk test.
The results of Levene's test indicated that the assumption of homogeneity of variances was met in all datasets for F1 ANOVA and in 90% of the datasets for F2 ANOVA.
However, the Shapiro-Wilk test revealed that the normality assumption was satisfied only in 15% of the datasets for F1 ANOVA and 70% for F2 ANOVA.
These findings suggest that using choice proportions as the dependent variable in ANOVA frequently violates the normality assumption, particularly in studies with small sample sizes.
We observed notable differences in the proportion of non-singular fits across random-effects structures (Table 4).
text.formatted: We observed notable differences in the proportion of non-singular fits across random-effects structures (Table <ref type="table" target="#tab_3">4</ref>).

text.text: The models with random intercepts only (RI and 2RI) and the model with random slopes for repetition for subjects and random intercepts for items (RS) resulted in non-singular fits in 100% of the datasets.

The model with random slopes for repetition and status for subjects and random intercepts for items (RSS), which was selected most often by AIC (see below), and the model with random slopes for repetition for both subjects and items (2RS) were non-singular in 75% of the datasets.
In contrast, the most complex model (3RS), despite being theoretically desirable (Barr et al., 2013), was non-singular in only 55% of the datasets, even in those with a large number of observations.
text.formatted: In contrast, the most complex model (3RS), despite being theoretically desirable <ref type="bibr" target="#b7">(Barr et al., 2013)</ref>, was non-singular in only 55% of the datasets, even in those with a large number of observations.

text.text: The model with complex random intercepts (CRI) was non-singular in only 25% of the datasets.
We determined the most appropriate random-effects structure by comparing GLMMs with varying specifications using AIC and BIC, considering only non-singular fits.
According to AIC, the best-performing model in 9 datasets assumed random slopes for repetition and truth status for subjects (RSS), but only random intercepts for items.
The most complex model (3RS) was selected in 4 datasets, and this model had the smallest mean AIC across all datasets, closely followed by RSS (mean ∆AIC = 2.24; (Table 4).
text.formatted: The most complex model (3RS) was selected in 4 datasets, and this model had the smallest mean AIC across all datasets, closely followed by RSS (mean ∆AIC = 2.24; (Table <ref type="table" target="#tab_3">4</ref>).

text.text: The model with random slopes for repetition for subjects and random intercepts for items (RS) was selected in 5 datasets, and the model with random slopes for repetition for both subjects and items (2RS) in 2 datasets.
BIC results differed slightly, favoring the model with random slopes for repetition for subjects and random intercepts for items (RS) in 9 datasets.

The second-best model, selected in 8 datasets, included random slopes for both repetition and status for subjects, and random intercepts for items (RSS), which had the smallest mean BIC across all datasets (Table 4).
text.formatted: The second-best model, selected in 8 datasets, included random slopes for both repetition and status for subjects, and random intercepts for items (RSS), which had the smallest mean BIC across all datasets (Table <ref type="table" target="#tab_3">4</ref>).

text.text: Additionally, the model with random intercepts for both subjects and items (2RI) was preferred in 2 datasets, while the model with random slopes for repetition for both subjects and items (2RS) was optimal only in 1 dataset (see supplementary materials for the dataset-specific values).

Overall, the model selection results provide clear empirical support for including random slopes of repetition for subjects, while there was more ambiguity regarding the inclusion of random slopes for the other factors.

The model with random intercepts and slopes of repetition and status for subjects and random intercepts for items (RSS) was selected both by AIC and BIC in 6 datasets, and the model with random slopes of repetition for subjects and and random intercepts for items (RS) in 4 datasets.
In one dataset, the model with random intercepts and slopes of repetition for both subjects and items (2RS) was selected by both AIC and BIC.
There was no other agreement between AIC and BIC for any other model in the datasets.
Table 4 also shows R² for all GLMM versions.

text.text: Conditional R² c values, which reflect variance explained by both fixed and random effects, were substantially larger than marginal R² m values, indicating that subject-and item-level variability accounted for a considerable proportion of variance.
As expected, both conditional and marginal R² values increased with model complexity in each dataset.

Note that the average values in Table 4 do not strictly follow this ordering, because conditional R² c could not be computed for models with singular fits or convergence failures and was thus excluded.

text.text: For example, although the complex random intercepts model (CRI) has the highest R² values, the computed values are from only a very small subset of the datasets, as CRI resulted in singular fits in most datasets.
Overall, differences in R² among GLMM specifications were small, both overall and within individual datasets (see supplementary materials).
The estimated size of the repetition effect was very similar across GLMM versions.
The mean of the probit coefficients ranged from 0.262 (Range: [-0.034, 0.589]) in the random intercepts for subjects only model to 0.297 (Range: [-0.043, 0.698]) in the most complex model.
Parameter means and ranges were almost identical in those models including at least one random slope term.

More generally, all estimated coefficients (including repetition) were very similar across GLMM versions, with mean probit values ranging from 0.072 (Range: [-1.593, 1.336]) in the random intercepts for subjects only model to 0.076 (Range: [-1.820, 1.414]) in the model with random slopes for repetition for subjects and random intercepts for items.
The mean of the estimated coefficients increased slightly from the simplest model (0.072) to the model with random slopes for repetition for subjects and random intercepts for items (0.076).
However, further increases in model complexity (i.e., adding multiple random slopes) did not change the fixed-effect estimates on average, which remained within a very narrow range (0.075 -0.076).
These patterns indicate that the fixed-effect estimates were relatively stable across different specifications of the random effects.

Figure 6 compares the fixed-effects estimates of the two-step SDT approach and the GLMM with random intercepts and slopes of repetition for subjects, and random intercepts for items (RS model).
text.formatted: Figure <ref type="figure" target="#fig_7">6</ref> compares the fixed-effects estimates of the two-step SDT approach and the GLMM with random intercepts and slopes of repetition for subjects, and random intercepts for items (RS model).

text.text: Most of the estimates were closely aligned between the two methods.

Where the estimates differed, the GLMM yielded estimates of larger magnitude for discrimination ability d ′ (i.e., the main effect of truth status) and, in several datasets, for the effect of repetition on the response bias c.

This is in line with the advantage of GLMMs that they model item variability directly instead of aggregating judgments across items, which attenuates SDT estimates in the two-step approach (Morey et al., 2008; Rouder et al., 2007).
text.formatted: This is in line with the advantage of GLMMs that they model item variability directly instead of aggregating judgments across items, which attenuates SDT estimates in the two-step approach <ref type="bibr" target="#b65">(Morey et al., 2008;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b80">Rouder et al., 2007)</ref>.

text.text: Moreover, in one dataset (i.e., Nadarevic et al., 2021 Study 3), the two-step SDT approach resulted in an extreme estimate of the effect of repetition on discrimination ability (about -1.3), whereas the GLMM yielded an estimate close to zero.
text.formatted: Moreover, in one dataset (i.e., <ref type="bibr" target="#b68">Nadarevic et al., 2021</ref> Study 3), the two-step SDT approach resulted in an extreme estimate of the effect of repetition on discrimination ability (about -1.3), whereas the GLMM yielded an estimate close to zero.

text.text: However, as we do not know the ground truth, it is not possible to conclude which model is more accurate.
As a remedy, we performed a simulation study.

The simulation study evaluated the performance of the different methods for binary judgments for data with a fully crossed, mixed factorial design with participants and items as crossed random factors.
We generated datasets mimicking typical truth-effect studies in our reanalysis, in which participants judge the truth of new and repeated statements that are either true or false.
The simulation was run using the SimDesign package (v2. 25 Chalmers & Adkins, 2020), with R code and results being available at the OSF repository.
text.formatted: The simulation was run using the SimDesign package (v2. <ref type="bibr">25</ref> Chalmers & Adkins, 2020), with R code and results being available at the OSF repository.

text.text: The simulation used a full factorial design with four factors: number of subjects (50 or 100), number of items (40 or 80), true effect size of repetition (0 or 0.3), and true effect size of the repetition-status interaction (0 or -0.3), yielding 16 simulation conditions.

In each condition, 5,000 datasets were generated, where each subject responded to each item exactly once (a fully crossed subject-by-item design), with item order randomized independently per subject.
Item status (true vs. false) was fixed at the item level: the first -1.5 -1.0 -0.5 0.0 0.5 1.0 1.5 -1.5 -1.0 -0.5 0.0 0.5 1.0 1.5 Two-step SDT vs.

Repetition (new vs. repeated) was manipulated within subjects and balanced within each status category, such that each subject received an equal number of new and repeated true statements, and an equal number of new and repeated false statements.

Binary responses were generated from the GLMM version with the most complex random-effects structure (3RS), described in the Reanalyses section, where Φ is the standard normal cumulative distribution function.
The predictors repetition and status were sum-to-zero contrast-coded (+0.5 and -0.5), and responses were drawn from a Bernoulli distribution using a probit link function.
All data-generating parameters are summarized in Table 5.
text.formatted: All data-generating parameters are summarized in Table <ref type="table" target="#tab_4">5</ref>.

text.text: The fixed-effect coefficients played two different roles in the simulation: The effects of interests were determined by the design factors (repetition: β1 =0 or 0.3; interaction: β3 = 0 or -0.3), allowing us to directly assess Type I error and power for the effects targeted by the analysis.

The non-manipulated parameters, the intercept (β 0 ) and the status effect (β 2 ), were not fixed at specific values but drawn independently for each simulated dataset from uniform distributions bracketing empirically plausible values.
All simulation values were determined based on the average and ranges of parameter estimates in the reanalyses of truth-effect datasets (see supplementary materials for details).
This was done so that the conclusions generalize across a plausible range observed in prior model fits to real data.

Subjects were assigned correlated random intercepts and random slopes for repetition and status (u 0i , u 1i , u 2i ), and items were assigned correlated random intercepts and random slopes for repetition (v 0j , v 1j ).
Items did not receive a random slope for status because status is a between-item factor.
Subject and item random effects were drawn from a three-and a two-dimensional normal distribution, respectively.

For each simulated dataset, standard deviations and correlations of these random effects were independently sampled from uniform ranges (similarly as in Barr et al., 2013) centered on mean parameter values obtained from our empirical reanalysis, and the resulting correlation matrices were converted to covariance matrices.
text.formatted: For each simulated dataset, standard deviations and correlations of these random effects were independently sampled from uniform ranges (similarly as in <ref type="bibr" target="#b7">Barr et al., 2013)</ref> centered on mean parameter values obtained from our empirical reanalysis, and the resulting correlation matrices were converted to covariance matrices.

text.text: Since independent random sampling of pairwise correlations does not guarantee that the three-dimensional covariance matrix is positive semi-definite, each generated matrix was checked via eigendecomposition 4 and, where necessary, corrected to the nearest positive-definite matrix before random effects were drawn from a multivariate normal distribution.
Finally, to emulate realistic data loss, a random proportion of responses between 0% and 5% was set to missing (completely at random) in each simulated dataset.
We fitted the same models described in the Reanalyses section to each dataset generated in the simulation.

The most complex model (3RS) corresponds to the true, data-generating model whereas all other, less complex GLMM versions make incorrect, simplifying assumptions regarding the random-effects structure.
Non-singular fits were most common for the intercepts-only models (RI and 2RI; above 99.9%), followed by the models with random slopes for subjects only (RS: 92.5%; RSS: 53.2%).
Non-singular fits were least common for the more complex models 2RS, 3RS and CRI with 50.9%, 29.0% and 7.7%, respectively.
5 Unless stated otherwise, Type I error rates, power, bias, and RMSE were computed across all replications, including singular fits.
Only in the model selection analyses with AIC and BIC, we additionally report results after excluding singular fits.
Figure 7 presents Type I error rates for the main effect of repetition and the repetition-status interaction across the four sample-size combinations.
text.formatted: Figure <ref type="figure">7</ref> presents Type I error rates for the main effect of repetition and the repetition-status interaction across the four sample-size combinations.

text.text: For the main effect, models based solely on random intercepts (RI and 2RI) and the by-items F2 ANOVA showed severe inflation (.162 -.315), worsening markedly as the number of items increased, while min-F ′ was overly conservative throughout (.013 -.026).
In contrast, F1 ANOVA remained close to the nominal level for the main effect (.057 -.074).

For the interaction, the pattern shifted, such that F1 ANOVA became the most inflated test (.080 -.126), 4 Covariance matrices for subject random effects were positive definite in 80.04% of generated datasets.

5 The normality assumption was met in 46.4% of the datasets for F1 ANOVA and in 85.8% for F2 ANOVA. increasing with the number of subjects, whereas F2 ANOVA showed more moderate inflation (.054 -.075) and GLMMs with random intercepts only (RI and 2RI) showed somewhat reduced, though still high error rates (.070 -.112) relative to the main effect.
Min-F ′ statistics remained markedly conservative for the interaction as well (.006 -.015).

Across both effects, GLMMs with random slopes of repetition for both subjects and items (2RS) plus random slopes of status for subjects (3RS) consistently produced error rates closest to the nominal α level (main effect: .057 -.063; interaction: .054 -.062), showing minimal sensitivity to sample size.
GLMMs with complex random intercepts (CRI) also remained reasonably well calibrated across both effects (main effect: .069 -.076; interaction: .059 -.070).

In contrast, GLMMs with random slopes for subjects only (RS and RSS) were anti-conservative, more strongly so for the interaction (.074 -.100) than for the main effect of repetition (.066 -.080), with Type I error rates increasing with the number of subjects.
The two-step SDT approach showed a similar inflation (main effect: .064 -.081; interaction: .072 -.099).
The reason is that these methods do not account for item-specific deviations in the repetition effect (i.e., the random slope v 1j of repetition for items).
Since truth status is a between-item factor, the repetition-status interaction is estimated by comparing the repetition effect between the sets of true and false items.
Hence, item-specific variability in the repetition effect directly adds to the sampling variability of the interaction estimate.

Ignoring this variance component (as in RS, RSS, F1 ANOVA, and the two-step SDT approach) results in standard errors that are too small and, in turn, in inflated Type I error rates, especially when the number of subjects is large relative to the number of items.
Since 2RS, 3RS, and CRI resulted in singular fits most often, one might suspect that their good calibration depends on whether the fit was singular.
To check this directly, we computed Type I error rates separately for non-singular and singular fits.

For 2RS and 3RS, Type I error rates based only on non-singular fits were at or slightly below the nominal level (main effect: .043 -.062; interaction: .044 -.052), whereas singular fits had slightly higher rates (main effect: .060 -.066; interaction: .058 -.069).
Thus, the good calibration of these models is not an artifact of selecting non-singular fits.

Instead, singular fits of 2RS and 3RS were slightly anti-conservative, but still much closer to the nominal level than RS and RSS, whose Type I error rates were similarly inflated for non-singular fits (main effect: .060 -.078; interaction: .072 -.101).

Figure 8 shows that for the main effect, power increased primarily with number of subjects (e.g., F1 ANOVA: .829 -.875 with 50 subjects to .959 -.976 with 100 subjects), and the random-intercepts-only models (RI, 2RI) and F2 ANOVA showed the highest power (.943 -.999), though this reflects their inflated Type I error rather than genuine sensitivity.
text.formatted: Figure <ref type="figure" target="#fig_8">8</ref> shows that for the main effect, power increased primarily with number of subjects (e.g., F1 ANOVA: .829 -.875 with 50 subjects to .959 -.976 with 100 subjects), and the random-intercepts-only models (RI, 2RI) and F2 ANOVA showed the highest power (.943 -.999), though this reflects their inflated Type I error rather than genuine sensitivity.

text.text: For the interaction, power ranged from .275 (min-F ′ , smallest sample) to .992 (RSS, largest sample).

Unlike the main effect, RS and RSS showed the highest power for the interaction (.634 -.992), slightly exceeding RI and 2RI (.612 -.985) and clearly exceeding F1 and F2 (.582 -.983), while min-F ′ again showed markedly the lowest power.
The two-step SDT approach also showed comparable power with the GLMMs (.634 -.986).

The models with the best-calibrated Type I error (2RS, 3RS, and CRI) showed power for the interaction (.608 -.981) comparable to, though marginally lower than, RS and RSS, indicating that stricter control over Type I error did not come at a substantial cost to power once the number of subjects reached 100.
Note that the higher power of RS and RSS for the interaction partly reflects their inflated Type I error rates.
As for Type I error rates, power was computed across all replications, including singular fits, which occurred most often for 2RS, 3RS, and CRI.

Overall, this should be considered when weighing these models' suitability to specific applications, since high singularity rate limits the practical applicability of otherwise well-calibrated models in real datasets with comparable sample sizes.
We also investigated model selection of GLMM versions using AIC and BIC.
The most complex 3RS model was the true data-generating model, so selection of other GLMMs means that simpler models achieve comparable statistical performance for the given sample sizes.
We first conducted model comparisons after excluding singular fits.
The results showed that the RS model was the winning model in 32.8% of the simulated datasets according to AIC, followed by RSS (28.7%) and 3RS (13.2%).
For BIC, RS was again the winning model most often, in 47.1% of the simulated datasets, followed by 2RI (26.3%) and RSS (19.6%).
We repeated the analysis while including all models regardless of whether the fit was singular.
