Figure B1 in Appendix B shows the average bias of the fixed-effect estimates, that is, the mean deviation of the estimated parameters from their true simulation values.
text.formatted: Figure <ref type="figure" target="#fig_3">B1</ref> in Appendix B shows the average bias of the fixed-effect estimates, that is, the mean deviation of the estimated parameters from their true simulation values.

text.text: Overall, bias was unaffected by the number of participants and items.
Therefore, we report bias averaged across the four sample-size conditions.
When the true effects of repetition and the interaction were zero, all models were essentially unbiased (absolute bias below .005).

If the effects were nonzero, the GLMM with random intercepts for subjects only (RI) showed the largest bias, underestimating the magnitude of the repetition (-0.032) and interaction effects (0.033 for a true effect of -0.3).
It was followed by the GLMM with random intercepts for subjects and items (2RI; -0.012 and 0.013) and the two-step SDT approach (2S-SDT; -0.008 and 0.006).
In contrast, the GLMMs with random slopes and complex random intercepts (RS, RSS, 2RS, 3RS, and CRI) were close to unbiased (absolute bias of about .004 or less).

The same ordering emerged for the non-manipulated fixed-effects parameters (intercept and status), with RI underestimating the status effect (i.e., d ′ ) most strongly (-0.055), followed by 2RI (-0.023) and 2S-SDT (-0.013).
Because bias does not capture the variability of estimates, we additionally examined the root mean squared error (RMSE) of the fixed-effect estimates (Figure B2 in Appendix B).
text.formatted: Because bias does not capture the variability of estimates, we additionally examined the root mean squared error (RMSE) of the fixed-effect estimates (Figure <ref type="figure" target="#fig_10">B2</ref> in Appendix B).

text.text: RMSE was affected mainly by the design and only to a small degree by the model version.

For all parameters, RMSE decreased with more participants and more items, whereas differences between models within a design cell were small (typically below .01 for the intercept, repetition, and interaction).

Doubling the number of items had the strongest effect on the non-manipulated parameters of intercept and status estimates, whereas doubling the number of participants had a larger effect on the repetition estimates.
For the interaction, both factors reduced RMSE substantially.
The random-slope models, which were nearly unbiased, yielded almost indistinguishable RMSE values that were slightly higher than those of the simpler models.
RI and 2RI often had the lowest RMSE for the intercept, repetition, and interaction despite their larger bias.
This advantage was most pronounced when the true effect was zero, where all models were practically unbiased, indicating that the simpler models produce less variable estimates.
For nonzero effects, this advantage diminished as bias increased.
In the largest design (100 participants, 80 items), RI had the highest RMSE for both the repetition and interaction estimates.
For status, RI performed clearly worst with 80 items.

The two-step SDT approach (2S-SDT) achieved RMSE values comparable to those of 2RI and was among the lowest for the non-manipulated intercept and status effects, but ranked between the random intercepts only (RI and 2RI) and more complex models (3RS and CRI) for the manipulated repetition and interaction effects.

We compared analysis approaches for binary judgments that differ in terms of aggregation level and analytic focus: repeated-measures ANOVA of choice proportions, two-step SDT, and GLMMs of dichotomous responses.

Besides discussing their theoretical assumptions and practical implementation, we compared these approaches empirically using a multiverse analysis (Steegen et al., 2016) by reanalyzing 20 truth effect studies with openly available data.
text.formatted: Besides discussing their theoretical assumptions and practical implementation, we compared these approaches empirically using a multiverse analysis <ref type="bibr" target="#b92">(Steegen et al., 2016)</ref> by reanalyzing 20 truth effect studies with openly available data.

text.text: We complemented our reanalysis of real data with a simulation study in order to provide practical guidance for analyzing binary judgments in psychological research.
In the reanalyses, the truth effect was robust, and the overall pattern of p-values was similar across methods.

F1 and F2 ANOVA yielded highly correlated p-values, whereas min-F ′ was more conservative: Of the 58 effects that were significant in both F1 and F2 ANOVA, ten (17.2%) were not significant for min-F ′ , seven of which involved repetition.
GLMMs with random intercepts only yielded markedly smaller p-values than F1 ANOVA, whereas adding random slopes of repetition for subjects yielded comparable p-values.
Adding further random slopes changed p-values, fixed-effect estimates, and explained variance only slightly, but frequently resulted in singular fits (3RS: 45% and CRI: 75% of the datasets).
Accordingly, AIC and BIC mostly selected models with random slopes for subjects but only random intercepts for items (RS and RSS).
The simulation showed that methods ignoring major sources of random variance were anti-conservative.
F2 ANOVA and GLMMs with random intercepts only (RI and 2RI) showed inflated Type I error rates for the main effect of repetition, which varied mainly across subjects.

F1 ANOVA, the two-step SDT approach, and GLMMs with random slopes for subjects only (RS and RSS) showed inflated Type I error rates for the repetition-status interaction (up to .126, .099, and .100, respectively), because they ignore item-specific variability of the repetition effect.

GLMMs with random slopes of repetition for both subjects and items (2RS and 3RS) kept Type I error rates closest to the nominal level, whereas min-F ′ was overly conservative and had the lowest power.
As in the reanalyses, these more complex GLMM versions frequently showed singular fits and were rarely selected by AIC and BIC.
These results qualify the common arguments against aggregated analyses.

Although the normality assumption was frequently violated in the reanalyses, F1 ANOVA kept Type I error rates close to the nominal level for the main effect of repetition, in line with the robustness of ANOVA for dichotomous data (Lunney, 1970).
text.formatted: Although the normality assumption was frequently violated in the reanalyses, F1 ANOVA kept Type I error rates close to the nominal level for the main effect of repetition, in line with the robustness of ANOVA for dichotomous data <ref type="bibr" target="#b56">(Lunney, 1970)</ref>.

text.text: The main limitation of F1 ANOVA and the two-step SDT approach was rather that they ignore item variability, just as F2 ANOVA ignores subject variability, whereas combining both via min-F ′ ensures generalizability only at the cost of power (Richter, 2006).
text.formatted: The main limitation of F1 ANOVA and the two-step SDT approach was rather that they ignore item variability, just as F2 ANOVA ignores subject variability, whereas combining both via min-F ′ ensures generalizability only at the cost of power <ref type="bibr" target="#b78">(Richter, 2006)</ref>.

text.text: Hence, the main advantage of GLMMs is not that they resolve violations of distributional assumptions, but that they account for random variability across subjects and items simultaneously.

Regarding the random-effects structure of GLMMs, both studies showed that random slopes of repetition for subjects are essential, which provides converging evidence with previous studies showing pronounced interindividual differences in the truth effect (Schnuerch et al., 2021; Zajdler & Schnuerch, 2026).
text.formatted: Regarding the random-effects structure of GLMMs, both studies showed that random slopes of repetition for subjects are essential, which provides converging evidence with previous studies showing pronounced interindividual differences in the truth effect <ref type="bibr" target="#b85">(Schnuerch et al., 2021;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b99">Zajdler & Schnuerch, 2026)</ref>.

text.text: The role of random slopes for items is less obvious, since corresponding GLMM versions were rarely selected by AIC and BIC and often resulted in singular fits.
However, omitting random slopes for items inflated Type I error rates for the interaction in the simulation study.
This apparent contradiction is resolved by the assumed size of the item variance.
The standard deviation of the random slopes of repetition for items was small (σ v1 ≤ 0.27, compared to σ u 1 up to 0.92 for subjects).
Such a small variance component improves the likelihood only slightly, which is easily outweighed by the penalty of AIC and BIC, and it is often estimated to be zero (resulting in a singular fit).

Nevertheless, assuming random slopes for items matters for testing the interaction of repetition and the between-item factor truth status, which is estimated by comparing repetition effects between the sets of true and false items.
Thus, model selection by AIC or BIC does not protect against inflated Type I error rates.

Similarly, the small item variance is consistent with the hypothesis that repetition increases perceived truth to a similar degree for all statements (Fazio et al., 2019, but  see Aktepe   and Heck, 2025), but it does not imply that random slopes for items can be omitted without consequences for statistical inference.
text.formatted: Similarly, the small item variance is consistent with the hypothesis that repetition increases perceived truth to a similar degree for all statements <ref type="bibr" target="#b29">(Fazio et al., 2019, but</ref>  <ref type="formula">see Aktepe   and Heck, 2025</ref>), but it does not imply that random slopes for items can be omitted without consequences for statistical inference.

text.text: Singular fits were therefore a practical rather than an inferential problem of the design-based models.

In the simulation, Type I error rates of singular fits of 2RS and 3RS were only slightly higher than those of non-singular fits and still much closer to the nominal level than those of RS and RSS (see supplementary materials).
GLMMs with complex random intercepts (Scandola & Tidoni, 2024) were also reasonably well calibrated, but resulted in singular fits most often.
text.formatted: GLMMs with complex random intercepts <ref type="bibr" target="#b82">(Scandola & Tidoni, 2024)</ref> were also reasonably well calibrated, but resulted in singular fits most often.

text.text: When estimating SDT parameters, GLMMs with random slopes were practically unbiased, whereas the two-step SDT approach and GLMMs with random intercepts underestimated the magnitude of the effects at a comparable RMSE.

This bias partly reflects that ignoring random variability on the latent probit scale, either by aggregating across items or by omitting random slopes, attenuates the estimates toward marginal effects, similarly as for the difference between marginal and conditional effects noted in the Reanalyses section.
The larger GLMM estimates of d ′ and of the repetition effect on c in the reanalyses are in line with this attenuation of two-step SDT estimates.
Based on our reanalysis and the simulation study, we recommend the following strategy for confirmatory hypothesis tests of binary judgments in crossed designs.
First, statistical methods should account for the main sources of random variance, that is, for subjects and items simultaneously.
F1 ANOVA, F2 ANOVA, and the two-step SDT approach do not meet this criterion, and min-F ′ has very low power.

Second, the random-effects structure of a GLMM should match the design, with random slopes for subjects for all within-subject factors and random slopes for items for all within-item factors (in truth-effect studies, the 3RS model).
Theoretical considerations and prior knowledge can help to identify the most relevant variance components, such as interindividual differences in the repetition effect.

Third, if such a complex model results in a singular fit, it can be simplified step by step, for instance, by first removing correlations and then variance components close to zero (Bates et al., 2018; Matuschek et al., 2017), possibly guided by AIC and BIC.
text.formatted: Third, if such a complex model results in a singular fit, it can be simplified step by step, for instance, by first removing correlations and then variance components close to zero <ref type="bibr" target="#b9">(Bates et al., 2018;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b60">Matuschek et al., 2017)</ref>, possibly guided by AIC and BIC.

text.text: However, a singular fit alone is not a strong reason to remove random slopes for items, and researchers should be aware that omitting random slopes for within-item factors can inflate Type I error rates for interactions of such factors with between-item factors (up to about .10 in our simulation).
The final random-effects structure and whether the fit was singular should be reported.
Fourth, SDT parameters should be estimated with probit GLMMs rather than with the two-step SDT approach.
Similar random-effects specifications can serve as a starting point when studying other psychological phenomena involving binary judgments.
Several limitations need to be considered.
The data-generating model in our simulation was the 3RS GLMM, which favors GLMMs, and this model in particular, by construction.
Moreover, all design factors had only two levels, so that the performance of the methods may differ for other data-generating mechanisms and more complex designs.

Our results may also not generalize to fields with larger item variability, such as psycholinguistics, where experimental materials cover only a small subset of the possible linguistic units (Baayen et al., 2008).
text.formatted: Our results may also not generalize to fields with larger item variability, such as psycholinguistics, where experimental materials cover only a small subset of the possible linguistic units <ref type="bibr" target="#b4">(Baayen et al., 2008)</ref>.

text.text: Moreover, we focused on frequentist methods, and future studies could investigate whether Bayesian mixed models also benefit from simpler random-effects structures.

Our study was also limited to binary judgments and did not include Likert ratings, which are ideally modeled using ordinal regression such as cumulative-link mixed models (Bürkner & Vuorre, 2019), an approach used only by very few truth-effect studies (e.g., Henderson et al., 2021).
text.formatted: Our study was also limited to binary judgments and did not include Likert ratings, which are ideally modeled using ordinal regression such as cumulative-link mixed models <ref type="bibr" target="#b16">(Bürkner & Vuorre, 2019)</ref>, an approach used only by very few truth-effect studies (e.g., <ref type="bibr" target="#b41">Henderson et al., 2021)</ref>.

text.text: Due to our focus on SDT, we did not consider alternative link functions such as the logit link (Luce, 2005), even though the choice of link function can affect the presence and size of certain effects (Aktepe & Heck, 2025).
text.formatted: Due to our focus on SDT, we did not consider alternative link functions such as the logit link <ref type="bibr" target="#b54">(Luce, 2005)</ref>, even though the choice of link function can affect the presence and size of certain effects <ref type="bibr" target="#b1">(Aktepe & Heck, 2025)</ref>.

text.text: Finally, we did not consider cognitive models such as evidence accumulation models (Pan & Hu, 2025) and multinomial processing tree models (Fazio et al., 2015; Schmidt & Heck, 2026), which decompose binary judgments into latent processes but rely on stronger assumptions and are computationally more demanding, especially as hierarchical models (Heck et al., 2018).
text.formatted: Finally, we did not consider cognitive models such as evidence accumulation models <ref type="bibr" target="#b73">(Pan & Hu, 2025)</ref> and multinomial processing tree models <ref type="bibr" target="#b28">(Fazio et al., 2015;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b84">Schmidt & Heck, 2026)</ref>, which decompose binary judgments into latent processes but rely on stronger assumptions and are computationally more demanding, especially as hierarchical models <ref type="bibr" target="#b40">(Heck et al., 2018)</ref>.

text.text: We compared widely used aggregated and trial-level statistical approaches for binary judgments in within-subject designs: repeated-measures ANOVA, a two-step SDT approach, and GLMMs, which automatically provide SDT estimates for discrimination ability and response bias when using a probit link function.

Our reanalyses of 20 openly available datasets on the repetition-based truth effect and a simulation study showed that methods ignoring the random variability of either subjects or items can result in inflated Type I error rates, whereas min-F ′ is overly conservative.
GLMMs account for differences between individuals and between items simultaneously.
Compared to the two-step SDT approach, GLMMs estimate discrimination ability and response bias with less bias, without requiring aggregation or corrections for extreme proportions.

GLMMs with a random-effects structure matching the design kept Type I error rates closest to the nominal level, but frequently resulted in singular fits, whereas simpler GLMMs with random slopes for subjects only were favored by AIC and BIC at the cost of inflated Type I error rates for interactions.

Overall, our findings highlight the benefits of GLMMs for binary judgments, with a random-effects structure that is based on the design and simplified only if necessary, while taking into account the consequences of such simplifications for hypothesis tests. 40 items 50 subjects 100 subjects RI 2RI RS RSS 2RS 3RS CRI 2S-SDT RI 2RI RS RSS 2RS 3RS CRI 2S-SDT 0.06 0.07 0.08 0.09 0.10 0.07 0.08 0.09 0.10 0.08 0.10 0.12 0.14 0.08 0.10 0.12 0.14 0.06 0.07 0.08 0.10 0.11 0.12 0.13 0.14 0.15 RMSE 80 items 50 subjects 100 subjects Repetition (true = 0) Repetition (true = 0.3) Interaction (true = 0) Interaction (true = -0.3) Intercept Status RI 2RI RS RSS 2RS 3RS CRI 2S-SDT RI 2RI RS RSS 2RS 3RS CRI 2S-SDT 0.06 0.07 0.08 0.09 0.10 0.07 0.08 0.09 0.10 0.08 0.10 0.12 0.14 0.08 0.10 0.12 0.14 0.06 0.07 0.08 0.10 0.11 0.12 0.13 0.14 0.15

text.text: subject) indicates that the model includes random intercepts for subjects (i.e., allowing the overall response level to vary between subjects).
Similarly, (1 | item) adds random intercepts for items.

Adding predictors inside the parentheses, such as (1 + repetition | subject), means that both the intercept and the slope of the factor repetition are allowed to vary across subjects, thereby capturing individual differences in how repetition affects judgments.

When multiple random terms are combined, as in (1 + repetition | subject) + (1 | item), the model accounts for random variation in both subjects and items.3 Furthermore, the colon : denotes an interaction between grouping factors, e.g., (1 | subject:repetition) denoting a unique intercept for each subject-repetition combination.

The slash, / in (1 | subject/repetition:status) expands to a nested grouping structure, so it includes subject-level random intercepts along with random intercepts for each subject-repetition-status combination (for more details seeBates et al., 2015; Scandola & Tidoni, 2024).

text.text: In our GLMM reanalyses, the following random-effects structures were fitted for each dataset: 1.
RI model: (1 | subject), specifying random intercepts for subjects only; 2.2RI model: (1 | subject) + (1 | item), specifying random intercepts for subjects and items; 3.
RS model:(1 + repetition | subject) + (1 | item), specifying random intercepts and slopes for repetition for subjects, and random intercepts for items; 4.

RSS model: (1 + repetition + status | subject) + (1 | item), specifying random intercepts and slopes for repetition and status for subjects, and random intercepts for items; 5.2RS model: (1 + repetition | subject) + (1 + repetition | item), specifying random intercepts and slopes for repetition for both subjects and items; 6.3RS model: (1 + repetition + status | subject) + (1 + repetition | item), specifying random intercepts and slopes for repetition and status for subjects, and random intercepts and slopes for repetition for items; 3 All models specified here allow for correlated random intercepts and slopes.
To specify models with uncorrelated random effects, researchers can use a double pipe (||) instead of a single pipe (|) in the model formula.7.

CRI model (complex random intercepts; Scandola & Tidoni, 2024): item/repetition), specifying random intercepts for subjects and items, as well as random intercepts for each combination of subject and repetition, subject and truth status, subject, repetition, and truth status, and item and repetition.

Comparison of GLMMs and F1 ANOVAFigure5shows p-values and log p-values for F1 ANOVA and the GLMM versions (plots showing only the effects of repetition, truth status, and their interaction can be found in the supplementary materials).
The model including only random intercepts for subjects resulted in smaller p-values.
Adding random intercepts for items did not address this issue.
However, additionally incorporating random slopes for repetition for subjects yielded p-values that were more comparable across GLMM and F1 ANOVA.
Hence, incorporating random slopes for repetition per subject is essential to ensure comparability between GLMM and F1 ANOVA.
Increasing model complexity further by adding random slopes of truth status for subjects and random slopes of repetition for items had only a minor impact on the results.
GLMMs with complex random intercepts were more conservative than ANOVA and other GLMM versions (see Appendix A), but also resulted in singular fits in most datasets (non-singular in only 25%)
